Chapter overview

Growth of Rationalism traces the development of Pagutharivu from earlier traditions of inquiry to modern anti-caste, scientific, feminist and post-Independence institutions, while distinguishing rationalism from atheism, secularism and related movements.

Meaning & foundationsIyothee Thass & SingaravelarPeriyar & social criticismPrint & public campaignsScience & legacy
Scope, Meaning and Forms of Rationalism

Rationalism or Pagutharivu examines claims through reason, evidence and human consequences, while remaining distinct from atheism, secularism and scientific temper.

Meaning of Rationalism

Rationalism gives priority to:

  • Reason
  • Evidence
  • Observation
  • Logical examination
  • Open questioning
  • Human experience
  • Willingness to revise beliefs

A rationalist does not accept a claim merely because it is:

  • Ancient
  • Sacred
  • Popular
  • Supported by tradition
  • Declared by a religious authority
  • Repeated by a political leader

The claim must be examined through evidence and its consequences for human life.

Pagutharivu

The Tamil word commonly used for rationalism is:

  • Pagutharivu

It may be understood as:

  • Analytical understanding
  • Discriminating knowledge
  • The ability to examine a matter critically
  • The capacity to distinguish truth from unsupported belief
Rationalism and Atheism

Rationalism and atheism are related but not identical.

Rationalism
  • A method of thinking
  • Demands evidence
  • Questions unsupported claims
  • Can be applied to religion, politics, medicine, caste and social customs
Atheism
  • Absence or rejection of belief in God or gods
  • A position concerning the existence of divine beings

A person may question superstition and religious authority while retaining some form of spiritual belief. Another person may adopt both rationalism and atheism.

Rationalism and Secularism
Rationalism
  • Concerns the method by which claims are examined
Secularism
  • Concerns the relationship between religion, state and public institutions
  • Requires equal citizenship regardless of religion
  • Opposes state discrimination based on faith
Rationalism and Scientific Temper

Scientific temper includes:

  • Curiosity
  • Evidence-based inquiry
  • Testing of claims
  • Acceptance of correction
  • Rejection of fraud and superstition

The Constitution of India identifies the development of scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform as a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(h).

Social Purpose in Tamil Nadu

Rationalism in Tamil Nadu developed mainly as a social movement rather than only as an abstract philosophy.

It was used to question:

  • Caste hierarchy
  • Untouchability
  • Religious privilege
  • Patriarchy
  • Child marriage
  • Denial of widow remarriage
  • Astrology
  • Superstition
  • Birth-based occupation
  • Unequal access to education
Earlier Traditions of Inquiry and the Modern Rationalist Break

Tamil society possessed earlier traditions of ethical inquiry and ritual criticism, but modern rationalism became an organised public movement under new colonial conditions.

Earlier Tamil Traditions

Tamil intellectual history contained several traditions that questioned ritual, status and external religious display.

These included:

  • Buddhist ethical thought
  • Jain traditions of debate
  • Siddhar poetry
  • Selected Bhakti criticism of empty ritual
  • Vallalar’s emphasis on compassion
  • Iyothee Thass’s Buddhist reinterpretation
  • Secular ethical reasoning in Tamil literature
Siddhar Tradition

Siddhar poems frequently criticised:

  • Empty ritual
  • Hypocritical religious conduct
  • Caste pride
  • Blind obedience
  • Excessive attachment to external symbols

Important Siddhars associated with critical social and religious expression include:

  • Sivavakkiyar
  • Pattinathar
  • Pambatti Siddhar
  • Kudambai Siddhar

However, Siddhars were not necessarily atheists in the modern sense. Many expressed mystical, yogic or spiritual ideas.

Buddhism and Jainism

Buddhist and Jain traditions contributed to:

  • Ethical debate
  • Logic
  • Non-violence
  • Criticism of ritual sacrifice
  • Monastic scholarship
  • Alternative explanations of morality

Iyothee Thass later used Buddhism to construct an anti-caste and casteless historical identity.

Vallalar

Vallalar criticised:

  • Caste exclusion
  • Hunger
  • Animal killing
  • Ritual without compassion

His Jeevakarunyam placed human and animal suffering above ritual status.

Vallalar remained a spiritual thinker and should not be described simply as an atheist rationalist.

The Modern Break

Modern rationalism differed from earlier critical traditions because it used:

  • Printing presses
  • Newspapers
  • Political organisations
  • Public conferences
  • Modern science
  • Secular education
  • Legislative reform
  • Mass propaganda

The modern movement converted individual criticism into an organised public campaign.

Historical Caution

There was no single uninterrupted rationalist organisation running from the Siddhars to Periyar.

Earlier traditions supplied critical ideas, while modern rationalism developed under new colonial and political conditions.

Education, Printing, Science and the New Public Sphere

Modern education, printing, science and translation created a public sphere in which inherited authority could be debated beyond restricted scholarly circles.

Modern Education

Colonial and missionary education introduced new fields of study, including:

  • Modern science
  • History
  • Geography
  • Political economy
  • Medicine
  • Mathematics
  • Comparative religion
  • Western philosophy

The new system also created:

  • Teachers
  • Lawyers
  • Journalists
  • Doctors
  • Government employees
  • Political speakers
  • Social reformers
Printing

The expansion of printing made it possible to circulate:

  • Classical texts
  • Religious criticism
  • Political speeches
  • Scientific explanations
  • Social-reform essays
  • Cartoons
  • Public debates
  • Conference resolutions

Printing reduced dependence on:

  • Palm-leaf manuscripts
  • Oral transmission
  • Temple-based learning
  • Restricted scholarly circles
Newspapers and Public Debate

Newspapers allowed reformers to:

  • Answer religious opponents
  • Question caste customs
  • Expose social injustice
  • Publish letters from readers
  • Report reform marriages
  • Criticise government policy
  • Translate global political and scientific ideas
Science and Social Criticism

Scientific developments encouraged people to seek natural explanations for:

  • Disease
  • Weather
  • Human reproduction
  • Evolution
  • Mental illness
  • Agricultural change
  • Physical phenomena

Rationalists argued that unexplained events should not automatically be attributed to:

  • Divine anger
  • Curses
  • Spirits
  • Fate
  • Astrology
Translation

Tamil translations introduced readers to:

  • European rationalism
  • Socialism
  • Materialism
  • Atheism
  • Anti-clerical thought
  • Revolutionary political writings

Translation also allowed Tamil activists to reinterpret global ideas according to local struggles involving caste, labour and gender.

New Public Sphere

The combination of education and print created a new public sphere consisting of:

  • Reading rooms
  • Associations
  • Political meetings
  • Public debates
  • Libraries
  • Journals
  • Street lectures
  • Theatre and cinema

This environment enabled rationalism to become a popular social language rather than remain an elite philosophical discussion.

Iyothee Thass and Ethical Anti-Caste Rationalism

Iyothee Thass combined historical inquiry, Buddhism and casteless Dravidian identity to construct an ethical anti-caste rationalism before Periyar.

Iyothee Thass

Pandithar Iyothee Thass lived from:

  • 1845 to 1914

He was known as:

  • Tamil scholar
  • Siddha medical practitioner
  • Journalist
  • Linguist
  • Buddhist thinker
  • Anti-caste intellectual
Critique of Caste

Iyothee Thass rejected the idea that caste hierarchy was natural or divinely ordained.

He argued that:

  • Birth could not determine human worth.
  • Untouchability was a constructed form of oppression.
  • Religious stories had been used to justify social domination.
  • Oppressed people should study their own history.
  • Education was essential for liberation.
Reinterpretation of History

He challenged dominant interpretations of:

  • Tamil history
  • Religion
  • Literature
  • Community identity

He argued that many oppressed Tamil communities were descendants of an older Buddhist society whose history had been suppressed.

This was not merely a religious conversion programme. It was a rational reconstruction of history intended to challenge caste identity.

Casteless Dravidian Identity

Iyothee Thass promoted the identity:

  • Casteless Dravidian
  • Sathi Petham Atra Dravidar

He opposed the automatic classification of oppressed communities as Hindus.

He argued that a community should not accept a religious identity that justified its degradation.

Sakya Buddhist Society

In 1898, Iyothee Thass founded the Sakya Buddhist Society in Madras.

It became an important centre for:

  • Buddhist study
  • Anti-caste organisation
  • Historical reinterpretation
  • Education
  • International Buddhist contact
Tamilan

Iyothee Thass used journalism to question:

  • Caste
  • Superstition
  • Religious domination
  • Colonial interpretation of Indian society

His weekly Oru Paisa Tamilan began in 1907 and was later known as Tamilan.

Ethical Rationalism

Iyothee Thass’s approach combined:

  • Ethical equality
  • Historical inquiry
  • Linguistic analysis
  • Buddhist thought
  • Anti-caste politics

Modern scholarship identifies him as a major founder of anti-caste Buddhist thought in modern India and as an important precursor to later Tamil rationalist politics.

Distinction from Periyar
Iyothee Thass
  • Recovered Buddhism as an egalitarian alternative
  • Reinterpreted oppressed communities as original Buddhists
  • Used historical and literary criticism
Periyar
  • Developed a more explicitly atheist and iconoclastic public movement
  • Rejected divine and scriptural authority itself
  • Used mass agitation, satire and political propaganda
Singaravelar: Science, Materialism and Labour Rationalism

Singaravelar linked scientific explanation and materialism with labour emancipation, socialism and opposition to fatalism.

M. Singaravelar

M. Singaravelar lived from:

  • 1860 to 1946

He was associated with:

  • Labour organisation
  • Socialism
  • Communism
  • Buddhism
  • Rationalism
  • Science communication
  • Anti-caste thought
Science and Social Change

Singaravelar argued that science should not remain confined to laboratories or elite education.

Science should help people understand:

  • Nature
  • Disease
  • Human evolution
  • Society
  • Labour
  • Economic exploitation

He used scientific explanations to oppose:

  • Superstition
  • Fear of divine punishment
  • Magical explanations
  • Religious fatalism
Materialism

Singaravelar increasingly adopted a materialist approach.

Materialism explained social conditions through:

  • Economic relations
  • Labour
  • Property
  • Production
  • Human institutions

It did not explain poverty or inequality as the result of:

  • Karma
  • Fate
  • Sin in an earlier birth
  • Divine will
Labour Rationalism

Singaravelar linked rationalism to working-class emancipation.

He argued that workers required:

  • Education
  • Scientific awareness
  • Organisation
  • Freedom from superstition
  • Understanding of exploitation

His rationalism therefore combined:

  • Scientific thinking
  • Class politics
  • Social equality
  • Anti-colonialism
Madras Atheists Conference

Singaravelar chaired an important atheists’ conference in Madras in December 1933.

His address, remembered under the title “The Death of God,” explained atheism and questioned religious explanations of social life.

Relationship with the Self-Respect Circle

From the early 1930s, Singaravelar contributed to publications connected with the Self-Respect Movement.

His writings appeared in journals such as:

  • Kudi Arasu
  • Revolt
  • Puratchi
  • Other reform publications

He helped bring socialist, scientific and materialist reasoning into Tamil rationalist discussion. Scholarship on his writings emphasises his attempt to popularise science for social change.

Essential Distinction

Singaravelar did not treat rationalism only as criticism of temples or religious rituals.

He connected it with:

  • Workers’ rights
  • Socialist organisation
  • Economic equality
  • Scientific education
Periyar’s Emergence as a Rationalist Critic

Periyar’s rationalist criticism emerged from caste discrimination, failures of representation and the defence of hierarchy through scripture and custom.

Early Public Life

E. V. Ramasamy, later called Periyar, lived from:

  • 1879 to 1973

His public career included:

  • Municipal administration
  • Congress politics
  • Non-Cooperation
  • Vaikom Satyagraha
  • Communal-representation campaigns
  • Self-Respect Movement
  • Justice Party leadership
  • Dravidar Kazhagam

The complete chronology belongs to Chapter 28.

Experiences That Shaped His Criticism

Periyar’s rationalist outlook developed through his encounters with:

  • Caste discrimination
  • Religious exclusion
  • Inequality within public institutions
  • Failure of political organisations to address communal representation
  • Patriarchal family practices
  • Scriptural defence of caste
  • Social acceptance of superstition
Exit from the Congress

Periyar left the Congress in 1925 after repeated failure to secure support for communal representation and because of wider disagreements concerning caste and social equality.

He increasingly argued that political independence without social equality would merely transfer power from one elite to another.

Rationalism as Social Liberation

For Periyar, rationalism required people to question:

  • God
  • Religion
  • Caste
  • Scriptures
  • Priestly authority
  • Patriarchy
  • Political leadership
  • Language myths
  • Nationalist symbols

He did not restrict criticism to private belief.

He asked whether a belief or institution:

  • Promoted equality
  • Protected dignity
  • Produced evidence
  • Benefited human beings
  • Maintained exploitation
Radical Humanism

Periyar treated human welfare as more important than:

  • Tradition
  • Religious command
  • Community honour
  • Scriptural authority
  • Divine reward

Tamil Nadu Open University teaching material describes his rationalism as a form of radical humanism and identifies his philosophy as iconoclastic and atheistic.

Chapter Boundary

This chapter covers the development of his rationalist method.

The following belong elsewhere:

  • Self-Respect organisation and conferences — Chapter 24
  • Self-Respect principles — Chapter 26
  • Complete biography and achievements — Chapter 28
  • Transformation of Justice Party and Dravidar Kazhagam — Chapters 25 and 28
Reason, Evidence and Human Welfare

Tamil rationalism evaluates authority through evidence, willingness to revise belief and its effect on equality, dignity and human welfare.

Questioning Authority

Rationalism requires that every claim be open to questioning.

No person should be treated as permanently beyond criticism because of:

  • Age
  • Religious status
  • Political power
  • Caste
  • Scholarship
  • Popularity
  • Family position
Evidence

A rational claim should be supported by:

  • Observation
  • Documents
  • Testable facts
  • Logical consistency
  • Reproducible results
  • Comparison with alternative explanations
Revision of Belief

Rationalism does not mean that a person can never make a mistake.

It requires willingness to:

  • Correct errors
  • Accept new evidence
  • Reject false information
  • Change conclusions
  • Distinguish belief from fact
Human Welfare

Tamil rationalists often evaluated customs through their effect on human beings.

A custom that caused:

  • Hunger
  • Humiliation
  • Untouchability
  • Violence
  • Ill health
  • Loss of education
  • Gender oppression

could not be defended merely because it was traditional.

Experience versus Authority

Direct human experience was given priority over:

  • Myth
  • Ritual claim
  • Astrological prediction
  • Hereditary privilege
  • Scriptural command
Rationalism and Ethics

Rationalism does not automatically mean absence of ethics.

Tamil rationalists grounded ethics in:

  • Equality
  • Justice
  • Compassion
  • Human dignity
  • Social responsibility
  • Freedom from exploitation
Rationalism and Democracy

Rationalist habits strengthen democracy by encouraging people to:

  • Question rulers
  • Examine propaganda
  • Reject personality worship
  • Demand evidence
  • Participate in informed debate
Rationalist Critique of Caste, Scripture and Priesthood

Rationalists treated caste, scriptural authority and hereditary priesthood as human institutions that could be examined and abolished.

Caste as a Human Institution

Rationalists rejected the claim that caste was created by divine authority.

They argued that caste was maintained through:

  • Social custom
  • Marriage restrictions
  • Religious texts
  • Occupational control
  • Education denial
  • Property inequality
  • Political power

If caste was a human institution, it could also be abolished through human action.

Varnashrama Dharma

Periyar and other rationalists criticised Varnashrama because it divided people by birth into graded social categories.

They argued that the system:

  • Denied equality
  • Restricted occupation
  • Controlled marriage
  • Justified untouchability
  • Protected hereditary privilege
Scripture

Rationalists asked whether sacred texts:

  • Supported caste hierarchy
  • Restricted women
  • Defended priestly privilege
  • Treated one group as superior
  • Encouraged irrational fear

They rejected the idea that a text must be accepted merely because it was considered sacred.

Priesthood

Hereditary priesthood was criticised because it linked religious authority to birth.

Rationalist demands included:

  • Equal access to religious knowledge
  • Removal of hereditary monopoly
  • Use of understandable language
  • Right of all communities to perform ceremonies
  • Marriage without compulsory priestly mediation
Untouchability

Rationalists argued that campaigns against untouchability were incomplete unless they also challenged:

  • Caste itself
  • Endogamy
  • Scriptural authority
  • Social segregation
  • Birth-based status
Anti-Brahminism and Anti-Brahminical Critique

A distinction is necessary.

Criticism of Brahminism
  • Criticism of a social and ideological system
  • Opposition to hereditary hierarchy and priestly domination
Hostility towards individuals by birth
  • Treating every individual as guilty because of caste birth
  • Inconsistent with individual equality

Periyar’s rhetoric often used the word Brahmin to describe both a privileged social group and Brahminical ideology, producing continuing debate about interpretation.

Social Objective

The rationalist goal was not simply to reverse the hierarchy.

It was to establish a society in which:

  • Birth did not determine status
  • Occupation was not hereditary
  • Education was open
  • Marriage was based on consent
  • Law treated citizens equally
Religion, Atheism, Iconoclasm and Freedom of Thought

Atheism and iconoclasm became public methods of challenging sacred authority, while freedom of thought also protected the equal rights of believers.

Criticism of Religion

Tamil rationalists criticised religion when it was used to support:

  • Caste
  • Gender inequality
  • Fear
  • Economic exploitation
  • Priesthood monopoly
  • Political obedience
  • Superstition

Their criticism could be directed at any religion, though the movement concentrated heavily on Hindu institutions because these shaped caste relations in Tamil society.

Atheism

Periyar publicly promoted atheism because he believed belief in divine authority sustained social obedience.

He argued that if God was used to justify caste, then questioning caste required questioning that concept of God.

Iconoclasm

Iconoclasm refers to public attacks on:

  • Sacred images
  • Religious symbols
  • Mythological authority
  • Ritual prestige

Rationalist campaigns sometimes used:

  • Breaking symbolic idols
  • Burning controversial texts or images
  • Satirical processions
  • Public debate
  • Provocative slogans

These actions were intended to remove fear surrounding sacred authority.

Purpose of Provocation

Supporters viewed provocative actions as a method to:

  • Encourage questioning
  • Challenge inherited fear
  • Expose unequal religious authority
  • Create public debate

Critics regarded them as:

  • Offensive
  • Unnecessarily confrontational
  • Hostile to religious freedom
  • Hurtful to believers

A balanced account should recognise both the reforming intention and the controversy produced by the method.

Rationalism and Religious Freedom

Freedom of thought includes:

  • Freedom to believe
  • Freedom not to believe
  • Freedom to change belief
  • Freedom to criticise religious institutions
  • Freedom from forced religious practice

Rationalism should not be confused with state persecution of believers.

Secular State

A secular state should not decide citizenship according to:

  • Religion
  • Caste
  • Belief in God
  • Ritual practice

Public policy should be based on:

  • Constitutional rights
  • Evidence
  • Equality
  • Public welfare
Essential Distinction
  • Atheism concerns belief in God.
  • Rationalism concerns how claims are examined.
  • Secularism concerns the relationship between religion and the state.
  • Humanism places human dignity and welfare at the centre.
Women, Marriage, Family and Bodily Autonomy

Rationalist social criticism extended to marriage, widowhood, chastity, property, employment, birth control and women’s bodily autonomy.

Rationalist Critique of Patriarchy

Rationalists argued that women’s subordination was protected through:

  • Religion
  • Family honour
  • Marriage customs
  • Property rules
  • Chastity expectations
  • Denial of education
  • Economic dependence
Marriage

Marriage was treated as a social agreement rather than an unchangeable sacred bond.

Rationalist arguments supported:

  • Consent of both partners
  • Inter-caste marriage
  • Widow remarriage
  • Divorce
  • Rejection of dowry
  • Marriage without compulsory religious ritual
  • Equal partnership

The complete practice of Self-Respect marriages belongs to Chapters 24 and 26.

Widowhood

Rationalists criticised customs that required widows to:

  • Remove ornaments
  • Wear restricted clothing
  • Avoid remarriage
  • Live under family control
  • Accept social isolation

They argued that widowhood should not destroy a woman’s right to ordinary life.

Chastity

Periyar criticised unequal standards that demanded chastity from women while permitting men greater freedom.

Rationalists argued for:

  • One ethical standard for all genders
  • Consent
  • Mutual responsibility
  • Freedom from sexual exploitation
Property and Employment

Women’s freedom required:

  • Education
  • Property rights
  • Paid employment
  • Independent income
  • Participation in public life
Birth Control and Family Planning

Periyar discussed birth control during a period when the subject was rarely addressed publicly.

He linked family planning with:

  • Women’s health
  • Economic independence
  • Freedom from repeated pregnancy
  • Ability to pursue education and work

Records of his publications place an early work on birth control around 1930.

Pen Yen Adimaiyanal?

Periyar’s work commonly translated as:

  • Why Were Women Enslaved?

examined:

  • Marriage
  • Chastity
  • Widowhood
  • Property
  • Religious control
  • Patriarchy

The full contribution of Periyar to women’s rights belongs to Chapter 28.

Rationalist Standard

A family custom should be judged according to whether it protects:

  • Consent
  • Equality
  • Health
  • Dignity
  • Freedom

not merely whether it is ancient.

Rationalist Journalism and Major Publications

Newspapers and journals carried rationalist, anti-caste, scientific and social-reform arguments to readers across Tamil society.

Importance of Journalism

Rationalism spread in Tamil Nadu mainly through:

  • Weeklies
  • Newspapers
  • Pamphlets
  • Translations
  • Cartoons
  • Conference reports
  • Reader correspondence

Publications reached people who could not attend movement conferences.

Kudi Arasu
  • Meaning — People’s Rule or Republic
  • Began — 2 May 1925
  • Language — Tamil
  • Founder and editor — Periyar

Kudi Arasu discussed:

  • Caste
  • Communal representation
  • Religion
  • Women’s rights
  • Self-respect
  • Rationalism
  • Politics
  • Labour

It became the principal early publication of Periyar’s social campaign.

Revolt
  • Began — 7 November 1928
  • Language — English
  • Place — Erode

Revolt carried the movement’s arguments to English-reading audiences in India and abroad.

It addressed:

  • Caste
  • Religion
  • nationalism
  • Women
  • Social reform
  • International political ideas

Nagammal was associated with its publication and printing.

Puratchi
  • Meaning — Revolution
  • Began — 1933

Puratchi appeared when Kudi Arasu faced colonial restrictions.

It continued discussion of:

  • Rationalism
  • Socialism
  • Anti-caste thought
  • Political repression
Pagutharivu
  • Meaning — Rationalism
  • Began — 1934

Sources differ over whether its first issue appeared on 12 January or 26 August 1934.

The important examination association is:

  • Pagutharivu — 1934 — Rationalism

It carried:

  • Rationalist essays
  • Scientific discussion
  • Social criticism
  • Tamil script reform

Periyar’s revised Tamil letters appeared through this publication.

Viduthalai
  • Meaning — Liberation
  • Began as a Justice Party publication in 1935
  • Later came under Periyar’s control
  • Developed into a Tamil daily

It became an important voice of:

  • Justice Party
  • Self-Respect thought
  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • Rationalism
  • Anti-caste politics
Unmai
  • Meaning — Truth
  • Began — 1970
  • Associated with Periyar’s later rationalist propaganda
The Modern Rationalist
  • Began — 1971
  • English publication
  • Founded by Periyar

It presented rationalist, humanist and anti-caste arguments to English readers.

High-Yield Publication Sequence
  • Kudi Arasu — 1925
  • Revolt — 1928
  • Puratchi — 1933
  • Pagutharivu — 1934
  • Viduthalai — 1935
  • Unmai — 1970
  • The Modern Rationalist — 1971
S. Ramanathan, Jeevanandham and Other Rationalist Voices

Rationalism grew through a wider network of organisers, translators, writers, labour leaders and women activists beyond its best-known leaders.

S. Ramanathan

S. Ramanathan was an important early associate in the Self-Respect and rationalist circle.

He contributed to:

  • Organisational work
  • Public conferences
  • Reform propaganda
  • English-language communication
  • Translation of international ideas

Detailed organisational history belongs to Chapter 24.

P. Jeevanandham

P. Jeevanandham lived from:

  • 1907 to 1963

His original name was:

  • Sorimuthu

He moved through several political and intellectual phases:

  • Gandhian nationalism
  • Anti-caste activism
  • Self-Respect Movement
  • Socialism
  • Communism
  • Tamil literary work
Why I Am an Atheist

Jeevanandham translated Bhagat Singh’s essay:

  • Why I Am an Atheist

into Tamil.

The translation circulated during the 1930s and was treated as a prohibited publication by the colonial government.

The work explained atheism as a reasoned position rather than an emotional rejection of religion.

Jeevanandham’s Rationalism

Jeevanandham linked rationalism with:

  • Anti-caste equality
  • Socialism
  • Labour organisation
  • Tamil literature
  • Secular education
  • Opposition to superstition

He later differed with Periyar on questions of:

  • Socialism
  • Nationalism
  • Political organisation
  • Movement strategy
Sami Chidambaranar

Sami Chidambaranar contributed as:

  • Tamil scholar
  • Journalist
  • Social reform writer
  • Supporter of rationalist interpretation

He used Tamil literature to question caste and religious hierarchy.

Kuthoosi Gurusamy

Kuthoosi Gurusamy became known as:

  • Journalist
  • Satirist
  • Rationalist propagandist
  • Editor associated with Dravidian publications

His sharp prose and humour made ideological criticism accessible to ordinary readers.

Bharathidasan

Bharathidasan used poetry to support:

  • Rationalism
  • Women’s equality
  • Tamil identity
  • Anti-caste thought
  • Social reform

His complete literary career belongs to Chapter 7.

Moovalur Ramamirtham

Moovalur Ramamirtham Ammaiyar criticised:

  • Devadasi exploitation
  • Patriarchy
  • Religious control of women
  • Social hypocrisy

Her role shows that rationalist social criticism was not limited to male thinkers.

Collective Importance

The rationalist movement grew through a network of:

  • Writers
  • Editors
  • Translators
  • Women activists
  • Labour organisers
  • Teachers
  • Public speakers

Periyar was its most influential mass leader, but he was not its only intellectual contributor.

Conferences, Public Campaigns and Rationalist Propaganda

Conferences, public debates, satire and symbolic campaigns converted rationalist thought into mass propaganda and social action.

Public Meetings

Rationalist meetings were conducted in:

  • Town halls
  • Village grounds
  • Market spaces
  • Marriage venues
  • Conference halls
  • Reading rooms
  • Labour centres

Speakers used ordinary Tamil rather than highly formal scholarly language.

Subjects Discussed

Public campaigns addressed:

  • God and religion
  • Caste
  • Untouchability
  • Astrology
  • Temple privilege
  • Women’s rights
  • Widow remarriage
  • Birth control
  • Education
  • Labour exploitation
  • Scientific knowledge
Conferences

Rationalist themes appeared through:

  • Self-Respect conferences
  • Atheist conferences
  • Women’s conferences
  • Non-Brahmin conferences
  • Labour gatherings
  • Dravidar Kazhagam meetings

The complete Self-Respect conference chronology belongs to Chapter 24.

Debates

Rationalists challenged religious scholars and social conservatives to public debate.

Debate topics included:

  • Existence of God
  • Scriptural authority
  • Caste origin
  • Astrology
  • Miracles
  • Priesthood
  • Women’s subordination
Demonstration of Natural Explanations

Rationalist propaganda attempted to show that supposed miracles could often be explained through:

  • Physical tricks
  • Chemical reactions
  • Sleight of hand
  • Suggestion
  • Fear
  • Coincidence
Satire

Satire was used to expose contradictions in:

  • Mythological stories
  • Ritual practice
  • Social hierarchy
  • Political leadership

Tools included:

  • Cartoons
  • Mock ceremonies
  • Theatre
  • Poems
  • Humorous essays
Symbolic Campaigns

Public symbolic actions included:

  • Opposition to religiously justified caste
  • Criticism of sacred texts
  • Anti-superstition demonstrations
  • Rejection of caste names
  • Marriage without priests
  • Public dining across caste barriers

Some activities overlapped with the Self-Respect Movement and should be treated in full only in Chapters 24 and 26.

Colonial Repression

Publications and speeches faced:

  • Security deposits
  • Confiscation
  • Prohibition
  • Sedition cases
  • Arrest
  • Imprisonment

The repeated replacement of prohibited journals by new publications demonstrated the movement’s dependence on print.

Public Response

Rationalist propaganda attracted:

  • Students
  • Non-Brahmin activists
  • Labour organisers
  • Women reformers
  • Dalit intellectuals
  • Socialist thinkers

It also faced strong opposition from:

  • Religious organisations
  • Conservative associations
  • Sections of nationalist leadership
  • Defenders of traditional caste institutions
Scientific Outlook, Education and Tamil Script Reform

Scientific outlook and script reform applied rationalist methods to health, education, literacy, printing and modern communication.

Scientific Outlook

Rationalists wanted science to become part of everyday life.

They promoted scientific explanations concerning:

  • Health
  • Sanitation
  • Disease
  • Reproduction
  • Astronomy
  • Evolution
  • Agriculture
  • Technology
Health

Rationalist health campaigns opposed reliance only on:

  • Ritual healing
  • Astrology
  • Magical objects
  • Curses
  • Spirit removal

They encouraged:

  • Medical treatment
  • Hygiene
  • Vaccination
  • Maternal care
  • Public sanitation
Education

Education was understood as more than literacy.

It should help students:

  • Question
  • Compare evidence
  • Reject caste prejudice
  • Understand science
  • Participate in society
  • Resist exploitation
Opposition to Myth as Science

Rationalists distinguished:

Mythology
  • Cultural or religious narrative
  • May carry symbolic value
Science
  • Requires observation
  • Testing
  • Evidence
  • Correction

They opposed presenting mythological stories as proven scientific history.

Tamil Script Reform

Periyar argued that Tamil writing should become:

  • Simpler
  • Easier to print
  • Easier to type
  • Easier to learn
  • Better suited to modern communication

He proposed reducing variant letter forms and simplifying selected compound characters.

Some revised characters appeared in Pagutharivu in the 1930s.

Objectives of Script Reform

The reform aimed to:

  • Reduce unnecessary complexity
  • Improve mass literacy
  • Simplify printing
  • Support typewriters
  • Modernise communication
Government Adoption

The Tamil Nadu government later adopted several of Periyar’s script reforms during his centenary period.

The complete political history of adoption is outside this chapter, but the reforms illustrate the practical side of rationalism.

Language and Rationalism

Periyar did not treat every old Tamil form as sacred merely because it was Tamil.

He argued that language should serve:

  • Education
  • Science
  • Equality
  • Communication
  • Social progress

This distinguished rationalist language reform from purely romantic language glorification.

Post-Independence Institutions and Rationalist Legacy

Post-Independence organisations and publications continued rationalist work because political freedom had not removed caste, superstition or gender inequality.

Continuity after Independence

Indian independence did not end rationalist activity.

Rationalists argued that political freedom had not automatically removed:

  • Caste
  • Untouchability
  • Superstition
  • Gender inequality
  • Religious exploitation
  • Unequal education
Dravidar Kazhagam

Dravidar Kazhagam continued rationalist propaganda through:

  • Public meetings
  • Publications
  • Conferences
  • Educational institutions
  • Anti-caste campaigns
  • Atheist activity

The organisation’s complete history belongs to Chapter 25.

Periyar Self-Respect Propaganda Institution

The Periyar Self-Respect Propaganda Institution was established and registered in:

  • 1952
  • Registration date — 23 September 1952

Its objectives included preserving and spreading:

  • Self-respect
  • Rationalism
  • Social equality
  • Periyar’s writings
Publications

Post-Independence rationalist publications included:

  • Viduthalai
  • Unmai
  • The Modern Rationalist
  • Books
  • Pamphlets
  • Translations
  • Conference proceedings
Periyar Rationalist Library

A rationalist library and research centre was established in 1974 after Periyar’s death.

It collected:

  • Periyar’s writings
  • Dravidian movement documents
  • Rationalist publications
  • Social-reform literature
  • Historical material
World and National Conferences

Tamil Nadu became an important venue for:

  • Atheist conferences
  • Rationalist conventions
  • Humanist meetings
  • Anti-superstition campaigns

These gatherings connected Tamil rationalism with wider Indian and international networks.

Constitutional Scientific Temper

Article 51A(h) strengthened the public importance of:

  • Scientific temper
  • Humanism
  • Inquiry
  • Reform

The constitutional language does not require citizens to become atheists. It requires development of a questioning and reform-oriented outlook.

Public Impact

Rationalist ideas influenced debate concerning:

  • Reservation
  • Caste names
  • Marriage
  • Temple administration
  • Women’s education
  • Family planning
  • Language
  • Social welfare
  • Scientific education
Limitations

Rationalism did not eliminate:

  • Caste practice
  • Astrology
  • Religious commercialisation
  • Gender discrimination
  • Personality worship
  • Political superstition

The continued existence of these practices shows that ideological influence and everyday social behaviour do not always change at the same speed.

Historical Assessment

The Tamil rationalist movement achieved its greatest influence when it connected reason with:

  • Social justice
  • Human dignity
  • Education
  • Women’s rights
  • Labour rights
  • Political representation

Its importance lies not only in disbelief in God but in making inherited authority open to public examination.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, thinkers, publications, concepts and distinctions frequently tested in TNPSC examinations.

Essential Chronology
  • 1845 — Birth of Iyothee Thass
  • 1860 — Birth of M. Singaravelar
  • 1879 — Birth of Periyar
  • 1898 — Iyothee Thass founded the Sakya Buddhist Society
  • 1907 — Oru Paisa Tamilan began
  • 1914 — Death of Iyothee Thass
  • 1925 — Kudi Arasu began
  • 1925 — Emergence of the Self-Respect Movement
  • 7 November 1928 — Revolt began
  • 1930 — Periyar’s early birth-control publication
  • 1933 — Puratchi began
  • December 1933 — Singaravelar chaired the Madras atheists’ conference
  • 1934 — Pagutharivu began
  • 1934–1935 — Jeevanandham’s Tamil translation of Why I Am an Atheist circulated and faced colonial prohibition
  • 1935 — Viduthalai began as a Justice Party publication
  • 1946 — Death of Singaravelar
  • 1952 — Periyar Self-Respect Propaganda Institution registered
  • 1963 — Death of P. Jeevanandham
  • 1970 — Unmai began
  • 1971 — The Modern Rationalist began
  • 1973 — Death of Periyar
  • 1974 — Periyar Rationalist Library inaugurated
  • 1976 — Scientific temper included in Article 51A(h) through the Forty-Second Amendment
Thinker–Association
  • Iyothee Thass — Buddhism, anti-caste historical inquiry and Tamilan
  • Singaravelar — science, materialism, labour and atheists’ conference
  • Periyar — mass rationalism, anti-caste criticism and rationalist publications
  • S. Ramanathan — early Self-Respect and rationalist organisation
  • P. Jeevanandham — Tamil translation of Why I Am an Atheist
  • Sami Chidambaranar — Tamil scholarship and rationalist writing
  • Kuthoosi Gurusamy — journalism, satire and propaganda
  • Bharathidasan — rationalist and social-reform poetry
  • Moovalur Ramamirtham — rationalist criticism of women’s exploitation
Publication–Year Associations
  • Kudi Arasu — 1925
  • Revolt — 1928
  • Puratchi — 1933
  • Pagutharivu — 1934
  • Viduthalai — 1935
  • Unmai — 1970
  • The Modern Rationalist — 1971
Publication–Language
  • Kudi Arasu — Tamil
  • Revolt — English
  • Puratchi — Tamil
  • Pagutharivu — Tamil
  • Viduthalai — Tamil
  • Unmai — Tamil
  • The Modern Rationalist — English
High-Yield Distinctions
Rationalism versus Atheism

Rationalism

  • Method of examining claims
  • Uses reason and evidence

Atheism

  • Absence or rejection of belief in God

A rationalist may be an atheist, but the two words do not mean exactly the same thing.

Rationalism versus Secularism

Rationalism

  • Method of thought

Secularism

  • Equal citizenship and separation of religious privilege from state power
Rationalism versus Scientific Temper

Rationalism

  • Broad critical examination of beliefs and institutions

Scientific temper

  • Evidence, experiment, inquiry and willingness to revise conclusions
Reform versus Rationalism

Reform

  • Changes an existing practice

Rationalism

  • Questions the basis and evidence of the practice itself

A reformer may retain religious belief; a rationalist may question religious authority more fundamentally.

Iyothee Thass versus Periyar

Iyothee Thass

  • Buddhist reinterpretation
  • Casteless Dravidian identity
  • Historical and literary criticism
  • Tamilan

Periyar

  • Explicit atheism
  • Mass public propaganda
  • Iconoclasm
  • Kudi Arasu and later publications
Iyothee Thass versus Singaravelar

Iyothee Thass

  • Buddhism and caste history
  • Ethical equality
  • Oppressed-community identity

Singaravelar

  • Science and materialism
  • Labour politics
  • Socialism and atheism
Singaravelar versus Periyar

Singaravelar

  • Scientific popularisation
  • Labour and socialist rationalism
  • Madras atheists’ conference

Periyar

  • Mass anti-caste rationalism
  • Self-Respect and Dravidian organisations
  • Wider social propaganda
Periyar versus Jeevanandham

Periyar

  • Principal mass rationalist leader
  • Anti-caste and Dravidian social politics

Jeevanandham

  • Rationalism combined with socialism and communism
  • Translated Why I Am an Atheist
Kudi Arasu versus Pagutharivu

Kudi Arasu

  • Began in 1925
  • Broad political and social journal

Pagutharivu

  • Began in 1934
  • Explicitly named Rationalism
  • Scientific, social and script-reform content
Revolt versus Puratchi

Revolt

  • English
  • Began in 1928

Puratchi

  • Tamil
  • Began in 1933

Both names convey revolutionary change but served different language audiences.

Self-Respect Movement versus Rationalist Movement

Self-Respect Movement

  • Organised social movement
  • Marriage, caste, gender and dignity
  • Detailed in Chapters 24 and 26

Rationalist movement

  • Wider method and intellectual campaign
  • Reason, evidence, atheism, science and criticism of authority

Rationalism was a central foundation of Self-Respect, but it extended beyond that single organisation.

Anti-Religious Criticism versus Religious Persecution

Anti-religious criticism

  • Freedom to question belief and institutions

Religious persecution

  • Denial of rights to people because of belief

Rationalist freedom of thought does not justify denying believers equal citizenship.

Mythology versus Science

Mythology

  • Cultural, symbolic or religious narrative

Science

  • Evidence-based and testable explanation

A myth may have literary importance without being treated as verified scientific history.

Script Reform versus Pure Tamil Movement

Script reform

  • Simplification of written letter forms
  • Printing, typing and literacy

Pure Tamil Movement

  • Reduction of Sanskrit-derived vocabulary
  • Language identity

They addressed different aspects of language.

Core Rationalist Questions

For any claim, ask:

  • What is the evidence?
  • Can it be tested?
  • Is there another explanation?
  • Who benefits from the belief?
  • Does it protect equality?
  • Does it cause harm?
  • Is it accepted because of fear?
  • Can the conclusion be revised?
Exam Traps
  • Rationalism and atheism are related but not identical.
  • Pagutharivu is the Tamil term commonly associated with rationalism.
  • Iyothee Thass preceded Periyar.
  • Iyothee Thass used Buddhism as an anti-caste historical alternative.
  • Singaravelar connected science with labour emancipation.
  • Singaravelar chaired an important Madras atheists’ conference in 1933.
  • Periyar did not begin his career directly as the leader of an atheist movement.
  • Kudi Arasu began in 1925.
  • Revolt was an English publication begun in 1928.
  • Puratchi is associated with 1933.
  • Pagutharivu is associated with 1934.
  • Viduthalai began in 1935.
  • Jeevanandham translated Bhagat Singh’s Why I Am an Atheist into Tamil.
  • The Modern Rationalist began in 1971.
  • Scientific temper is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(h).
  • Siddhar criticism of ritual should not automatically be described as modern atheism.
  • Vallalar was a spiritual reformer, not simply an atheist rationalist.
  • Rationalism was a foundation of the Self-Respect Movement, but the two are not identical.
  • The complete Self-Respect Movement belongs to Chapter 24.
  • Self-Respect principles belong to Chapter 26.
  • Periyar’s complete contribution belongs to Chapter 28.
